drops.label: Drop 1 - Sun 10:00 AM ET: the address
drops.theme: You already run a business. The missing part is an address, not a skill.
drops.headline: You just don't own the address.

copy.facebook_instagram:
You already run a business.

You know what to charge. You know which customers come back and which ones were never going to. You know what a slow week means and what to do about it. None of that came out of a textbook.

The part that is missing is not a skill. It is an address.

Right now people find you through somebody else's app, somebody else's feed, somebody else's search box. The work is yours. The address it happens at belongs to a company you have never met.

A domain name is that address. You register it in your own name, and everything else hangs off it: your page, your contact form, your booking link. That is the whole idea.

Here is how a domain actually works, in plain words:
https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/what-is-a-domain-name/

Web Basics is a one-time $199 for the first year. That is one focused website, a full year of managed hosting, and your domain registered for you, or the one you already own connected. After the first year it is $9.99 a month, plus what the domain costs to renew.

drops.label: Drop 2 - Mon 6:30 PM ET: the client list
drops.theme: Access is a permission. A permission is not a possession.
drops.headline: Access is a permission.

copy.facebook_instagram:
The list is the business.

Every name in it you earned one at a time. A first appointment that went well. A referral. Somebody who came back after six months because you remembered what they wanted.

Here is the part worth checking. Depending on where that list lives, you can usually see it, you can often export some version of it, and you do not control it. Access is a permission a platform grants you, and a permission is not the same thing as a possession.

A name you cannot reach is a memory, not a client list.

This is not an argument for leaving anywhere. It is an argument for keeping a second copy somewhere that answers to you: your own page, your own contact form, your own inbox.

There is a fifteen-minute audit here that tells you exactly where you stand:
https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/who-owns-your-client-list-booking-app/

drops.label: Drop 3 - Wed 8:30 AM ET: the price
drops.theme: You already know your prices. There is nowhere public that says them.
drops.headline: So why does everyone ask?

copy.facebook_instagram:
You already know your prices.

You worked them out the hard way: what the job takes, what the materials cost, what your time is worth, what people will actually pay. You can price a job in your head while your hands are busy.

So why does every new customer still have to ask?

Right now the answer lives in your head and in your thumbs. Somebody messages "how much?", and at some point tonight you stop what you are doing and type it out again. The ones who did not want to ask never messaged at all.

A page does that first round for you. It says what you do, what it generally costs, and what happens next. It says it at 6am and at midnight, to people who would never have sent a message. You still quote the real number for the real job.

How a page answers the price question before it is asked:
https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/website-answers-price-questions-before-asked/

drops.label: Drop 4 - Thu 12:30 PM ET: taking the booking
drops.theme: A bookable page answers two questions and can leave the rest for later.
drops.headline: Two questions, answered.

copy.facebook_instagram:
A page that gets you booked is not a prettier version of your app profile. It has a different job.

On a marketplace, somebody has already decided to hire through that platform and is choosing between the listings in front of them. On your own page, they are deciding something more basic: whether to hire you at all.

So a bookable page really only has to answer two questions.

Can this person do the specific thing I want? Not the category. The exact job, named the way a customer would ask for it.

Can I trust them with it? Trust here is mundane. Will they answer. Will the price hold. Will they be where they said they would be.

Anything on the page that serves neither question can wait.

The full breakdown, including what you can safely leave off for now:
https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/what-a-bookable-page-actually-needs/

drops.label: Drop 5 - Sat 5:00 PM ET: what survives
drops.theme: Keep the accounts. Own one address that cannot be cleared.
drops.headline: Keep the accounts. Own one address.

copy.facebook_instagram:
Everything you have built is sitting on a surface somebody else can clear.

Not out of malice. A policy changes. An automated system flags an account. A platform decides a whole category of business no longer fits. You get an email, and years of posts, followers and history stop being reachable in an afternoon.

You already know this, because you have watched it happen to somebody.

The answer is not to leave anywhere. Keep the accounts. They work, and they are where people already are.

The answer is that one of the places people can find you should be a place that cannot be taken away: a page on a domain in your name, with your own contact details on it. Everything else can point at it.

What a link-in-bio page trades away, and what it does not:
https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/linktree-vs-real-website-what-you-trade-away/

drops.label: Drop 6 - Sun 11:00 AM ET: the paperwork
drops.theme: Not a new skill. Paperwork, with a published price and published boundaries.
drops.headline: Paperwork you have not done yet. $199 for the first year.

copy.facebook_instagram:
None of this is a new skill. It is paperwork you have not done yet.

You already handle the hard parts: pricing, demand, reputation, collecting money, getting people to come back. The formal side is smaller than it looks from the outside. A domain. A page that says what you do. Somewhere the request lands.

Web Basics is a one-time $199 for the first year. That covers one focused website, a full year of managed hosting, and first-year registration of a domain, or connecting the one you already own. After the first year it is $9.99 a month, plus whatever the domain costs to renew.

What it does not cover, said plainly: business email on your own domain is a separate product, and ongoing maintenance is an add-on. The scope is narrow on purpose, which is why the price can stay where it is.

The published boundaries, including how to tell when you have outgrown it:
https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/199-website-inclusions-and-boundaries/
